name: Functional appliance orthodontics

lead: Functional appliances are orthodontic devices, fixed or removable, that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children with a Class II bite, where the lower jaw sits behind the upper. The payoff people are after is a better bite and a stronger-looking profile. The best-known are the Herbst, Twin-block and Frankel appliances.

The appliance repositions the lower jaw and the resulting muscle forces are intended to influence jaw growth and tooth position. A fixed Herbst uses a telescoping rod that lets the mouth open but holds the jaw forward when closed. Randomized trials in children report favorable changes in many treated patients, and there is debate over how much of the change is skeletal versus dental. The trials concern adolescents, not adults.

paras: Treatment is run by an orthodontist during the growing years. Fixed designs like the Herbst are cemented in place, while removable ones like the Twin-block and Frankel depend on the child wearing them consistently. It is often followed by braces to finish the bite, and changes build over months of wear.

Reported drawbacks include initial discomfort, chewing difficulty, unwanted tooth spacing, and failure to complete treatment with removable designs that rely on wear. It is designed for growing patients with Class II bites; adult outcomes and effects on facial appearance are not covered by the trials found.

angle.text: Orthodontists use Herbst, Twin-block and similar appliances in growing children to bring the lower jaw forward in Class II cases, improving the bite and the profile. The appliance guides jaw growth, and trials show changes, with debate over how much is skeletal versus dental.

lead: Functional appliance orthodontics is a family of treatments, using devices such as the Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel (FR-2), Bionator, Bass and activator appliances, that aim to modify jaw growth and bite relationships in growing patients, most often to correct a Class II malocclusion where the lower jaw sits behind the upper.[1][2] For appearance, the goal is a better-balanced profile: by holding the lower jaw forward during growth, treatment aims to reduce overjet (prominent upper front teeth), improve the lower jaw's position relative to the upper and bring the chin and lower third of the face into better proportion.[3][2]

The Herbst appliance is a fixed device with a telescoping rod that holds the lower jaw forward; Emil Herbst developed it in the early 1900s and Hans Pancherz reintroduced it in 1979.[1] Twin-block, Frankel, Bionator and Bass appliances are removable.[3][4][5] A randomized trial of 215 patients aged 11 to 14 compared Herbst with Twin-block and found a lower failure-to-complete rate for the Herbst.[3] Randomized trials of early (preadolescent) Class II treatment report favorable growth changes in about 75% of treated children in one study,[2] and Cochrane reviews of the randomized evidence describe reductions in overjet and in the ANB angle (the front-to-back relationship of the jaws) with functional appliances, alongside a lower rate of broken front teeth when treatment starts early.[6]

Researchers and clinicians describe the changes as a mix of skeletal change (a little extra forward movement of the lower jaw, some restraint of upper jaw growth) and dental change (teeth tipping and moving); how much of the result is skeletal, and how much lasts to adulthood, remains discussed in the literature.[6][6] The trials concern growing children and adolescents; published research on adult facial appearance is absent. On looksmax.org, users ask whether Herbst-type appliances can lengthen a short mandible or improve the lower third of the face, and discuss alternatives and access to orthodontic care.[7][8]

paras: Class II malocclusion, in which the lower dental arch sits behind the upper, is commonly seen in orthodontic practice. A 1996 review describes it as occurring in about one third of the US population and notes its common components: a narrow upper jaw, a retruded lower jaw and increased lower anterior face height.[9] Functional appliances are one of several strategies for it, alongside headgear, fixed braces, extractions and, in adults, jaw surgery.

The appearance rationale is straightforward for orthodontists and patients alike: a recessed chin and prominent upper teeth change the lip posture and the profile line, and moving the lower jaw and teeth forward is intended to bring the profile closer to balance. Soft-tissue measures such as facial convexity and the angle between lower lip and chin (the mentolabial angle) are therefore commonly reported in trials.[6][6]

The term functional appliance reflects the original idea that the devices use the patient's own muscle action and nervous-system responses, rather than direct mechanical force on individual teeth, to produce orthodontic or orthopaedic change. Reviews of muscle function describe this as targeted exercise of the masticatory system, while noting that electromyographic and bite-force measurements show high variability and that the stability of results is not always adequate.[10]

The Herbst is a fixed appliance attached by stainless steel frameworks to upper molars and lower premolars, with telescoping rods that let the mouth open but hold the lower jaw forward when closed. Variants include cast, acrylic splint and ball-joint designs, versions combined with a palatal expander, and later bite-jumping designs such as the Sabbagh Spring, Powerscope and Cantilever Bite Jumper.[1] Fixed spring-type correctors such as the Forsus Fatigue Resistant Device occupy a similar niche.[6]

The Twin-block is a removable two-part appliance, with upper and lower plates that interlock to posture the jaw forward, and is designed to be worn nearly full time. The Frankel regulator (FR-2) is a removable appliance that works through the soft tissues of the cheeks and lips; the Bionator, Bass and activator are other removable designs.[3][4][5] Newer approaches include clear-aligner mandibular advancement systems, which a 2026 meta-analysis found produced skeletal changes not significantly different from the Twin-block, with slightly greater overjet reduction, though the evidence was mostly retrospective.[6]

Historical reviews from 1980 and 1983 document the development of functional jaw orthopedics in Europe, from the early work of Andresen, Haupl and others, and the later modifications that spread to the United States.[11][12]

Orthodontists describe functional appliances as altering the position of the mandible so that muscle forces and joint adaptation change the growth relationship of the jaws and teeth. Studies have examined effects on the teeth, skeleton and the glenoid fossa of the temporomandibular joint.[13][14] The Herbst's effects on the masticatory system were studied with casts, cephalometric x-rays and muscle electromyography.[15]

CBCT studies pooled in a 2026 systematic review (seven studies, 258 patients) found that Twin-block increased condylar volume and forward positioning, Herbst produced modest condylar changes with stable condyle-fossa relationships, and glenoid fossa remodeling was inconsistent.[6] A separate 2026 review of joint imaging found disc position generally stable and no new disc displacement or new-onset temporomandibular symptoms, rating the certainty of evidence low to very low.[6]

The Herbst's continuous action is said to shorten active treatment to about 6 to 8 months, compared with 2 to 4 years for removable alternatives, and it does not rely on patient cooperation; starting at or just after the pubertal growth peak is associated with more stable results, although some researchers found similar results before and after puberty.[1] A retrospective study of Twin-block patients reported that those treated at the pubertal peak showed more favorable mandibular growth and chin projection at postpubertal follow-up than those treated before it.[6]

The Herbst is described as used to correct a Class II malocclusion from a set-back mandible, and also in patients with deep overbite, mandibular midline deviation or mouth breathing, and in some post-adolescent patients who may benefit from residual growth.[1]

Timing is a central debate. Randomized trials compared early (mixed dentition) with adolescent treatment; the Cochrane reviews reported that, after both groups finished treatment, final overjet and jaw relationship were similar, while early treatment was associated with fewer injuries to prominent front teeth.[6][6] Functional appliances alone were also compared with no treatment in adolescence, where the 2018 review reported overjet reductions of about 5 mm with fixed and about 4.6 mm with removable appliances, with only removable appliances showing a reduction in ANB.[6]

Functional appliance research also extends beyond appearance: a 2023 meta-analysis found that functional orthopedic appliances improved apnea-hypopnea index, oxygen saturation and OSA-18 questionnaire scores in children and adolescents with obstructive sleep apnea.[16]

According to Wikipedia, fixed Herbst appliances can cause upper-arch spacing and initial discomfort or chewing difficulty during the first weeks, which typically resolves; more severe underbites may need longer treatment.[1] Removable appliances depend on the patient wearing them, and not all patients complete treatment.[3] A 2026 comparison of Twin-block and Forsus devices reported that the Forsus produced more dentoalveolar change, especially forward tipping of the lower incisors.[6]

Studies have examined the temporomandibular joint during Class II treatment, including disc-condyle relationships with a functional advancer.[17][6] Appliance treatment is carried out by orthodontists, who assess growth stage and bite before choosing a device.[1]

Early treatment trials. A 2-phase randomized trial of early Class II treatment (overjet over 7 mm) found favorable growth changes in about 75% of children treated early with headgear or a functional appliance; after the second phase of fixed appliances, outcomes in early and later-treated groups were compared.[2] A 1997 controlled trial randomised mixed-dentition patients with overjet of 7 mm or more to early treatment or observation to test whether skeletal pattern changes.[18] A related randomized report on early Class II intervention was published the following year.[19]

Cochrane reviews. The 2007 review (8 trials, 592 children) found that early functional appliance or headgear reduced overjet and ANB during the first phase but that the effect was not sustained once second-phase treatment was complete.[6] The 2013 update (17 studies, 721 participants) and the 2018 update (27 randomized trials, 1,251 participants) found no clear advantages of early over adolescent treatment other than reduced incisor trauma, and reported low-quality evidence that adolescent functional appliance treatment reduces the prominence of upper front teeth compared with no treatment.[6][6] Twin-block was associated with a slightly larger ANB reduction than other appliances (about 0.56 degrees), and removable appliances with a greater ANB reduction than fixed ones (about 1.04 degrees), while fixed appliances gave greater overjet reduction.[6]

Herbst and Twin-block. The UK multicenter randomized trial of Herbst versus Twin-block in 215 patients aged 11 to 14 found a lower failure-to-complete rate with the Herbst.[3] A 2026 meta-analysis of seven randomized trials (548 participants) found both appliances effective with generally similar skeletal and soft-tissue effects, with modest Herbst advantages in the mentolabial angle and molar relationship.[6] A cephalometric comparison followed Twin-block and stainless steel crown Herbst appliances with fixed appliance therapy.[20] A double-blind study of 56 pubertal Class II patients compared a bonded Herbst protocol with a headgear protocol, each followed by fixed appliances.[21]

Soft tissue and profile. A 2025 randomized trial in 52 pubertal patients found that both aesthetic and conventional Twin-block appliances improved facial convexity and the mentolabial angle, with the conventional version causing lip retraction relative to the E-line that the aesthetic version did not.[6] A 2026 pooled analysis of six studies (276 patients) reported that removable and fixed appliances corrected Class II through a combination of skeletal and dental changes, with low to moderate certainty of evidence.[6]

Other comparisons. Studies compared Twin-block and Frankel with an untreated Class II sample, compared Herbst with Frankel, and compared the hard-tissue effects of Bass, Bionator and Twin-block.[4][5][14] A study of 48 adolescents with cephalometric signs that predicted an unfavourable response treated them with functional jaw orthopedics followed by fixed appliances and compared them with matched controls.[22]
No studies found on effects of functional appliances on adult facial appearance.

Appearance-focused forums discuss functional appliances mainly in relation to recessed or short lower jaws, overbite and the lower third of the face. Typical threads ask whether Herbst, Twin-block or Bionator appliances change the lower third, whether a Herbst might recess the maxilla, whether Forsus (a fixed bite-corrector) can be used without an overbite, and what alternatives exist for people who cannot access orthodontic care or whose budget is limited.[7][8][23][24][25]

Users frequently weigh appliances against other routes to a better chin and jaw line, including fillers, genioplasty and other jaw surgery. Posters who are teenagers describe seeking an appliance before growth ends, reflecting the growth-stage emphasis in orthodontic literature.[7][8]

The Frankel regulator is also discussed within orthotropics, the approach founded by British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025), who in 1958 proposed that malocclusion is a postural problem rather than an inherited one and who, after visiting Rolf Frankel in 1968, developed his own method with palatal expansion, diet change and a specific tongue posture.[26] Mew preferred such appliances and palatal expansion to extractions and headgear.[26]

Mainstream orthodontists oppose his views on the cause of malocclusion. In 2010 the General Dental Council reprimanded Mew over advertising, and in 2017 revoked his licence over false advertising and patient confidentiality breaches.[26] His son Mike Mew and he popularised the do-it-yourself oral posture practice called mewing, which spread on social media from about 2019, and which Wikipedia describes as unproven, with the American Association of Orthodontists saying it has no evidence of improving the jaw.[27] A looksmax.org thread discusses Mike Mew on Frankel regulators.[28]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and related forums, functional appliances are discussed as a route to a longer or more forward lower jaw and a better lower third, especially by teenagers, and compared with fillers, surgery and mouth-guard alternatives.[7][8]

timeline.event: Emil Herbst develops the bite-jumping appliance.[1]
John Mew proposes that malocclusion is a postural rather than inherited problem, the seed of orthotropics.[26]
Hans Pancherz reintroduces the Herbst appliance.[1]
A historical review traces functional appliance development in Europe.[12]
Pancherz publishes a survey of the Herbst's biologic effects and clinical use.[15]

Outcomes of a 2-phase randomized trial of early Class II treatment published.[2]
